name: old cracked asphalt road of cool charcoal grey with fine scattered non-directional aggregate specks, faded slightly warmer patches, thin crack lines, soft stains and worn broken fragments of yellow and white lane paint, its unconnected edges broken off into dirt as a chipped asphalt lip with loose asphalt chunks, laid as a road network with crossroads and dead ends
label: wasteland_ruins/asphalt

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches on dirt ground (flat terrain tileset)

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain tileset: a full 256x192 sheet of brown dirt with charcoal asphalt road shapes (crossroads, dead ends, a large block) seen from directly above. The silhouette is a full-width rectangle on every row (0-191:256), and no standing volume, front face, eave line or ellipse is drawn. The dark road edges are chipped lips on the ground plane, not vertical faces. It is a ground texture, so there is no front face of 3 or more rows and the sheet reads as flat top-down.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt patches have only about 3 lightness steps: a mid charcoal, a darker speck and a lighter speck. The 12 distinct colours across the whole piece and the 5 visible tones per tile are fewer than the paving reference (7 visible tones). The brief also asks for yellow and white lane paint, warmer faded patches and soft stains. None of these show up, and the few thin crack lines are plain dark strokes. The dirt ground is mottled in 2-3 browns, a little richer than the asphalt but still shallow. The edges are chipped, but they read as a single dark rim whose tint is only partly material-coloured (16% neutral dark edge pixels), so I call the outline mixed. Large asphalt areas are mostly uniform speckle, with little per-chunk shading and no clear loose chunks. Overall it looks thinner and flatter than the Beodeul references at the same scale and would not sit well beside them.

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches on dirt ground (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends, a large slab)

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain tile sheet seen straight down: grey asphalt patches with chipped edges sit on a brown dirt field across the full 256x192 canvas. There is no standing volume, no front-edge line followed by eave shadow, no ellipse, and no south face. The only vertical-looking marks are short dark crack lines and the ragged chipped lip along the bottom edges of the patches, which are 1-2 rows of edge detail, not a front face. With no front face of 3 or more rows, it reads as a top-down slab, which is the expected form for terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt patches carry only about 3 grey steps: a mid charcoal, a darker speck tone and a few dark crack lines. The Beodeul paving reference has about 5-6 steps with per-stone shading and light edge highlights. The measured 5 visible tones per tile sits below the paving reference's 7. The dirt surround is a brown speckle with about 3 tones, which is comparable to the grass reference. The asphalt edges are lumpy and fairly dark, with slight tint, so I call the outline mixed. The brief asks for yellow and white lane paint, stains, warmer faded patches and loose chunks. None of these are visible, and the asphalt reads as a uniform grey slab with a few crack lines. The road network is sparse, with large dirt gaps and disconnected blobs, and it does not read as a clear 4x3 tileable road with crossroads. Near-flat coverage is low at 5%, so there are no big flat fills, but the aggregate texture is a uniform noise stipple with no clusters or per-stone shading. Overall it is shallower and flatter than the reference paving.

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches on dirt ground, flat terrain tile

answer.evidence: The image is a flat top-down terrain tileset: a full 256x192 brown dirt field with dark grey asphalt road shapes (a crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends, a large block and a small block) with chipped dirt edges. There is no standing volume, no front face, no eave, ellipse or roof. The column scans show only ground texture bands (dirt tones, darker crack/stain rows, the grey asphalt run at rows 53-62 and 117-126). As terrain it is a flat ground surface, so it has no front face and reads as a top-down slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt patches are shallow. They read as about 3 grey steps: a dark charcoal base, a slightly lighter speckle and a darker edge. The paving reference carries about 6-7 steps with per-stone shading. The measured 5 visible tones per tile sits between the grass reference (3) and the paving reference (7), so it is not far below. The asphalt interiors look flat, with sparse speckles and only a few thin dark crack lines. I see no warm faded patches, stains, or yellow and white lane paint, all of which the description asks for. The dirt surround has decent grain, but the road is the subject and it is the weaker part. The 'chipped lip' edges are just a dark, slightly tinted rim with few loose chunks. The 16% neutral edge share suggests the outlines carry some tint, but the edge does not read as a shaded material ramp. The layout is also unconvincing: the road pieces are isolated blobs and one large rectangle, not a connected network with crossroads and dead ends. Overall it falls short of the Beodeul standard in shading depth and texture variety.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt patches are a flat charcoal with a speckle of dots, so the main ramp has only about 3 steps (base, lighter speck, darker speck) against the paving reference's 5-6. The road shapes are small, isolated blobs, not a connected network, and I see no yellow or white lane paint, no stains and no warmer patches. Only a few thin dark crack lines show, and they are near-black strokes. The edge is a dark charcoal lip with little tint. Only 16% of dark edge pixels are neutral, but that comes mostly from the brown dirt around the patches, so the asphalt's own outline reads as dark grey rather than a dark tone of the material. The dirt field is speckled in 2-3 browns with little variation, and the chipped lip is only suggested. Measured values are 5 visible tones per tile, against 7 for the paving reference and 3 for the grass. Near-flat coverage is 5%, so there are no big flat fills. Density is close to the grass reference but below the paving, and the asphalt ramp is shallower than the Beodeul standard, so it fails.
